Besides what hath been said of this Quality in the former Vol. I must add here, Thar the Corpuscular Philosophy, before Sir 1 / - Newton's wonderful Improvement of it, did not to the Bottom of this Matter; for ic gave no count of the Cause of the chief Condition re quifite to constitute a Fluid Body, viz, the various Motions and Agitations of its Particles. But this may be in a good Measure accounted for, if you suppose it to be one of the Primary Laws of Nature, that as all Particles of Matter do attrap one another when they come within a certain Distance, so, at all greater Distances from one another, they do fly away from, and avoid one another. For then, though their common Gravity may keep them together in a Mass, together ( it may be sometimes) with the Pressure of other Bodies upon them; yet their continual Endeavour to avoid one another finglypand the adventitious Implies of Light, Heat, or other external Causes, may make the Particles of Fluids conti. nually move round about one another, and so produce this Quality. It is, indeed, a Difficulty Tcannor yet get over, to account for the Particles of Fluids always keeping at such a Distance from one another, as not to come within the Sphere of one another's Attraction. There has been a great Dispute amongst the Naturalists, how these Bodies came thus. formed, and a great many have been wery fond of ( what appears to me asa very absurd Opinion) viz. That these are only Lu / us Natura, only the Sports and Divers ions of Nature, to make her self merry in the dark Regions of the Earth. fibres.c: FIBRES. There are other Divisions and Distinctions of Fibres, besides those two mentioned in Vol. 1. For, according to some Authors, there are in an Animal Body, Carnous, Membranous, Cartaliginous, Tendinous, Offecus, and Nervous Fibres, according to the Matter of which they confit. The Carnous Fibres, of which the Flesh is composed, are vascular and hollow, being full of little Cells: They are called Fibremotices, because they are the chief Organs of Muscular Motion. There is a Difference also among Fibres, as to their Situation and Course. For those that run lengthwise in Right Lines, are called Strait Fibres: Those that run about some Part, as those do that form Sphinter Muscles, are call'd Circular, Those Fibres which cross Strait ones at Right An. gles are called Transverse; but those which inter ect them at any other Angles, Ob / que Fibres.
